title: The Government and the National Budget
summary: The three levels and three arms of government, the role of government in the economy, sources of government income, taxes, and how the national budget is drawn up and spent.

notes.caption: Three spheres (levels) of government
rows: Defence, foreign affairs, national roads, higher education, social grants
Water, electricity, refuse removal, sewerage, local roads, parks

notes.caption: Three arms of government (separation of powers)
rows: Parliament: the National Assembly and the National Council of Provinces
Carries out (implements) laws and runs the country
The President, Cabinet ministers and government departments
Interprets laws and judges whether they are broken
The courts, with the Constitutional Court as the highest court

notes.text: The role of government in the economy

items: Provides **public goods and services** that private businesses might not supply: roads, police, schools, hospitals, defence.
Collects **taxes** to pay for these services.
Makes **laws** to protect consumers, workers and the environment.
**Redistributes income** by taxing richer people more and giving **social grants** to the poor.
Creates conditions for economic growth and jobs.

notes.text: Where does government get its money?

rows: Individuals on their salaries (the more you earn, the higher the percentage: a **progressive** tax)
Consumers, added at **15%** to most goods and services (some basic foods are zero-rated)
On imported goods and on products like alcohol, tobacco and fuel ('sin taxes')

notes.text: Government can also borrow money (which creates **national debt**) and earn money from fees, fines and state-owned enterprises.
The government's financial plan for the year, showing its expected **income** (revenue) and planned **expenditure**.
The **Minister of Finance** presents the budget to Parliament every **February**. South Africa's financial year runs from **1 April to 31 March**.

items: **Budget surplus**: income is more than expenditure.
**Budget deficit**: expenditure is more than income (the usual situation in South Africa); the government borrows to cover the difference.

notes.text: The largest parts of South Africa's budget usually go to **education** (called learning and culture), **social development** (grants), **health**, and **paying interest on debt**.
